origin_region: Yunnan · Xishuangbanna · Mengla · Yiwu · state forest gardens
cultivar: Yunnan large-leaf (Camellia sinensis var. assamica), unpruned tall forest trees (gaogan) of old abandoned gardens
processing: Raw pu-erh: leaf carried out of the forest on foot, pan-fired, hand-rolled and sun-dried, then pressed lightly into small cakes or sold loose; batches are tiny and handled by hand throughout.
harvest_season: Spring (April, later than village gardens because of shade and altitude); only one or two pickings a year, and autumn forest tea is rare.
appearance_dry: Very long, dark, loosely twisted leaves with long buds and whippy stems, loosely pressed or left as maocha.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold with a thick, oily sheen, very clear.
appearance_wet: Long, thick, elastic leaves on long stems, dark olive, clearly from unpruned trees.
taste_profile: Yiwu honey and orchid turned up to forest intensity: a dense, oily body, a wild-honey and herb depth, very little bitterness, a cooling throat feel and a sweetness that keeps returning for minutes.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, briefly. Porcelain, short early steeps, and keep going: forest tea often peaks around steep five and runs well past twelve.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by named forest garden (Guafengzhai Chaping, Bohetang, Tongqinghe, Tianmenshan, Baichayuan, Wangong, Yishanmo, Baishahe), usually in 200 g cakes or loose lots from boutique producers, with 'guoyoulin' and 'gaogan' (tall trunk) as the price-raising words. The category only took off around 2014–2016, so there is a small amount of mid-aged state-forest tea from roughly 2012–2018 and no aged market; what is sold is young (1–5 years), 2015–2025, in dry storage. Prices are the highest in Yiwu, with Bohetang at the top, and because picking in protected forest is regulated and the trees are few, cheap state-forest tea is a contradiction in terms.
description:
'Guoyoulin' means state-owned forest, and in Yiwu it refers to tea trees growing inside protected forest reserves on the mountains above the villages, in gardens that were planted long ago, abandoned, and swallowed by the forest. Names like Guafengzhai Chaping, Bohetang, Tongqinghe, Tianmenshan and Wangong are all state-forest gardens, and since the mid-2010s they have been the most expensive tea in the Yiwu area.

The trees are unpruned and often tall, hence the related buzzword gaogan, and they grow in deep shade at around 1,300–1,700 m. Picking means a long walk in and out, so batches are tiny and everything is processed by hand in the normal sheng way, with a light press or no press at all. Access and harvesting inside the reserves are regulated, which limits supply further.

In the cup it is Yiwu amplified: a dense oily body, honey and orchid with a wild-honey and herb depth, almost no bitterness, a cooling throat sensation and a sweetness that keeps returning for minutes. Compared with village Yiwu it is thicker, wilder and longer. Short early steeps in porcelain, and do not stop at steep eight; this tea is still giving at twelve.

Sold by spring year and garden name in small cakes and loose lots, at prices from high to astonishing. The honesty problem is obvious: a few hectares of forest trees cannot supply every shop with Bohetang, so most 'guoyoulin' is village Yiwu or forest-edge tea with a borrowed name. Long unpruned leaves and that unmistakable thickness are the markers; a tea that is merely nice is not it.

If you want to taste the category without the gamble, Guafengzhai village tea or a good Mahei is the sane comparison, and the difference will tell you whether the forest premium is for you.
sources_note: The list of state-forest garden names and the mid-2010s start of the category are from trade reporting; regulations on picking inside protected forest have varied over time and are described only in general terms.
